p: Hi, my name is Paul. I just wanna—
Hi, Paul.
Hi, how are you?
Good.
Oh, gotta turn it on? No, sorry. I just wanna double back on your generator question.
Sure, go right ahead.
We have that generator. That generator is for Engine Company 295, specifically.
Oh, good.
Yes, yes.
I heard from them, yes.
Yes, that project is currently— the design is currently complete, and we are rolling right into construction at the beginning of FY27.
Oh, good. FY27, which means July 1st is FY27, so we can expect to see movement. I'll be paying attention right after July 1st.
Yeah, yeah.
For 285.
Yeah, so we've already reached out to all of our vendors and obtained their proposals and everything.

Thank you for that, I appreciate it. As far as the overall budget goes, I mean, we are in the process of signing a budget on June 30th of $124.7 billion. And anybody who knows me knows I'm in a bit of an uproar about that, because I like to see where the money's going. And you guys are certainly entitled to major upgrades

to your fire home— your firehouses, structurally, your vehicles. All around, you guys are entitled to pretty big— if we're going to increase the budget by $100– $14 billion total, if we're going to be increasing the budget to that kind of money, I just am curious, before I vote on the 30th, where's our money going?
So our FY27, expense budget is about $2.7 billion, and our capital budget going from '26 through '35 is about $1.9 billion.

Okay, so let's add up those two numbers, shall we? 9 point— nine plus seven is 16, carry it over, three, four– so that's $4.6 billion for the Fire Department out of $124.7 billion. I think that's outrageous. That's all I'll say about that. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Restler followed by J. Sanchez.
Not in a good way.

Tough act to follow. I'll do my best. Thank you to the chairs and

congratulations, Commissioner. Really excited to have you in this role and somebody who brings EMS expertise to the agency right now, I think is urgently needed. And I also just want to take a second to congratulate the promotion of my friend and most importantly constituent, Jason Shelly, Deputy Commissioner, very well deserved. He's been such an anchor in the Fire Department now for a decade plus. We're really lucky to have him there. So just a few questions. I've been deeply concerned by the fires that we've been seeing across our city. I know we've had a concentration of them in the Bronx that have been fatal, and it's terribly scary. And grateful for all the work that the members of FDNY do every day to keep us safe. But also wanna make sure that we're smartly investing resources, that can make the greatest difference to prevent fires from taking lives and ruining property. So just to confirm, Chief, I think— I believe that I heard in your testimony that we've got 20 engines right now that have a fifth firefighter that are deployed?
Yes, there are 20 engines.

And there's no data that we have whatsoever to show that a fifth firefighter improves or doesn't improve outcomes one way or the other, response times? No? Just to confirm, this is what you testified to earlier, I just want to get this clear.
Not response times, but we know that they stretch and operate hose lines quicker.

They stretch and operate hose lines quicker, but no impact on getting fires under control faster with the fifth person or not? We have no data to back this up. I mean, other than your anecdotal expertise.
Because we don't have that many five firefighter engines to see that.
Well, we have 20, but understood. If there's no data, there's no data. I just— what would the cost be, Deputy Commissioner Christoff, to adding a fifth firefighter citywide?
So we are currently in conversations with OMB on that point.
But it's an estimate that you should be able to come up with pretty directly. Could you give us a ballpark?
We would defer to the budget director, who I believe is testifying in the coming days.

You can't give us an estimate of what it would cost? We know how many firehouses there are, we know how many engines there are, there are no— I mean, right? Adding a 5th firefighter, what would that cost us? Ballpark?
I think—
[interposing] You know this number.
The council has cost estimates that are not out of line.
What are those estimates that the council has said? Could you get those to us just for the purpose of the conversation? What are the council's cost estimates?
We can follow up.

No, I— come on, we're at a hearing. We're asking basic questions. You know the answers to them, you should share them on the record. What are the council's cost estimates? I'm not even asking you to give the cost estimate. What's the cost estimate?

A council member has asked a direct question and he deserves an answer. So if you don't have it now, we have plenty of time to sit and wait, and then you can get that answer for him. It is rude to sit there and not answer a direct question from an elected official who came here today to represent his constituency, whether you like the question or not. So let's work on getting that information for Council Member Restler. I know you've signed up for a second round, Council Member Restler, but if you have other questions, please proceed.
I could do a third round too, if Chair– you know.
Okay. Council Member J. Sanchez.

I have lots of other questions to ask. I just am waiting because I

really do want an answer here, but we'll come back to it on the second round.
Oh, sorry, wait. Go ahead. Go for it.

I'm sorry. I don't mean to— I'll shift gears and I'll come back to my questions on the fifth firefighter later. Commissioner, we've had some challenges with FDNY and DOT coordination on bike lanes. Does the fire department support protected bike lanes?

Yeah. So we are a life-saving agency. That's our mission, our core mission, save lives. And we appreciate the fact that bike lanes put people in a safer place. And they save lives. So, yeah, the Fire Department has no problem with bike lanes.
Thank you. We–

[interposing] There are going to be these situations where maneuvering around them are an issue. And in those circumstances, as we have already started having conversations with the DOT to resolve those issues together.

And we sent you a letter to this effect, and I don't think we got a commitment on a time frame, but Council Member Ariola passed legislation requiring coordination between DOT and FDNY on bike lanes. There's been some litigation around this as well. Can we get a commitment from the Fire Department that barring extraordinary circumstances, the feedback can be provided to DOT within 30 days?

We are going to try our very, very best. Having these additional heads are definitely going to help speed things along, but sometimes they're just— you know, part of the— it's not only the process. It's not only the Fire Department, I would say, that kind of slows things down. It may be a more complex thing that needs to be reviewed. It takes a little longer. But we certainly will commit that we'll do our best to get them a timely response.
Okay.

And we're working very well together. I mean, we are talking together and solving problems together. And we

actually have seen— I can— have Chief Currao talk to you about it if you wish. But we have seen some reduction in turnaround times.

I– the chair asked me to be brief in this round and I've already gone over, but I'll just say appreciate the improved coordination. I think having a time frame commitment that, barring extraordinary circumstances or really complex project, that FDNY is getting back to DOT in a certain time frame really matters for planning and execution because there's a set time frame in the year for— you know, about 6 months, the DOT can install these projects, and we lose the windows and lose a year of safety that we can otherwise get if we're getting tight responsiveness from the Fire Department. So I hope we can work together to have some real accountability there.
Yeah, I can assure you we're working well together.
Thank you.
And, Council Member Restler, I have you on for round two, so don't worry.

Okay, so just quickly, we can agree that it is your job and your mission to put out fires, right? And you acknowledge that fires go out faster with the additional staffing. Do we agree on that? Yes or no?
Yes, as a general statement, yes.
Thank you.
Okay, Council Member J. Sanchez followed by P. Sanchez.

Thank you. First and foremost, I want to say thank you to all the firefighters for all for all the work that you do day in and day out. Also, happy Pride Month. I know nothing has to deal with sexuality, but representation matters, and there are people all over the city and this country that get to see someone like you and feel represented. So thank you for the work that you do as well. Aside from that, back to the fifth Firefighters. Representing the South Bronx and a proud co-chair of the Bronx delegation, this is truly important to us. We sent over a letter on February 10th, in partnership with Council Member

Ariola and the Bronx Borough President. But I want to dive deeper. You said there are already 20 fire stations that have this fifth firefighter, but they are dependent on the higher the buildings, the more firefighters. So is it safe to say that these 20 fire stations are located in downtown Brooklyn and Midtown Manhattan?

Some of them are, but it's not necessarily high-rise buildings, right? It's buildings that have longer hose line stretches. In high-rise buildings, we operate off a standpipe, which is generally a shorter stretch than stretching off the apparatus.
Is there— is there any way to identify where these 20 firehouses are? And–
[interposing] Yes, we have them, we can provide that for you.
How many of those are currently in the Bronx?
I'm not— do we have that, Kevin? Currently, four of the engine companies in the Bronx have five firefighters.
And how many engine companies are in the Bronx in total?
I think we have 30.
So, how many fires have happened in these areas that have the fifth firefighter already during the course of this past year?
I'll have to get that for you. So you're asking the number of fires that the engines where there are five firefighters, the number of fires they've gone to?
Yes.
Okay, we'll have to get that for you.
Thank you.

Can we have that by the second round? We need that information. We need the information answered. We asked you to come prepared, so saying we'll get the information is not going to be tolerated. Find the information, answer in the second round.
We have the breakdown of the engines and the fires they've had the last three fiscal years. Is that what you're asking for?

Basically, what I'm trying to get to with my line of questioning is have there been enough fires in where these fifth firefighters are to justify them being there? You said earlier that based on gaps in coverage that you would move the firefighters over to cover different things, and so—
We would move the fire companies around.

So based on the data that you already have based on the fires, has there been any indication that would suggest that moving some of the stations that have a fifth firefighter to other stations in the Bronx that are experiencing higher fires? Would there be any type of movement from the stations that are not experiencing fires versus the ones that are?
I guess we could have that discussion, but they're all going to fires.

Okay. But it's just– if the fifth firefighter is reducing times and reducing the ability— I completely understand that, you know, what's– the cause for the fire and the prevention is not a fifth firefighter. That's not what we're saying. The housing stock and the infrastructure, but we're not going to change the housing stock overnight. It's physically and literally impossible. But what we can do is cut down response times to what we actually do with the fires.

And I understand that question. But then you also have to see the reality that there's other council members here that if we take one of the five firefighter engines from their area, we're going to get the same— the same issue.

Well, I think just showing from Staten Island to Brooklyn to the Bronx, we're seeing a concerned unifying voice about the fact of everyone's recognizing the number of fires that the Bronx is going through. And we have been on this since the very beginning. I mean, I know this fight has been happening now for 15 years, but from when we started as the Bronx delegation

co-chair, this has been a major fight. So understanding that combating fire times in the Bronx is our top priority, and making sure that if there are other places that are not having a single fire or minimal fires compared to what we're experiencing every day— I get the all-hand— the notices every day on my email, multiple times a day. If we're able to move those firefighters around, that also does tremendous things for the ability to take care of our fellow Bronxites. So thank you.

Thank you. P. Sanchez? COUNCIL MEMBER P. SANCHEZ? Thank you. Thank you, cousin. It won't get old, maybe in a couple years. But thank you, Chair, for the unrelenting questions on the fifth firefighter. I have to– I have to join. Chief, I have to join Commissioner. But before I do that, I just want to echo my colleagues in thanking the FDNY, the firefighters who who jump at the flames, who are there. I feel like— I live right next to a battalion, and I feel like the fire— the sirens are just nonstop, nonstop. So, I thank you to our firefighters. I thank you to our EMS. But it does

feel like the Bronx is burning. It feels like the Bronx is burning again. And I uplift the 50 New Yorkers who we've had— or almost 50 New Yorkers who we've already lost this year. And highlighting, Chief, and I'd love some clarity in the— here during this hearing, that in a private briefing with the Bronx delegation some weeks ago, you shared that the fires have nearly doubled over the last three years in the Bronx and Queens, for the time period that we were in. So I'd love to just get updated numbers on that. And then specifically just want to— and I should highlight for you, I'm going to do the thing where I ask ask all my questions and then hopefully leave you five seconds to respond. But I just want to make sure to get them all in and I'm sure you'll be able to capture them. We had a fatal fire, at 2226 West Tremont last weekend. A one-year-old passed away on Bainbridge Avenue on the block where I grew up. And so it really feels in the Bronx and it feels like in my neighborhood that this is– it's just relentless. It's just relentless. In my view, I want to complicate our conversation also on the fifth firefighter. My view is that we need a three-pronged

approach. We need to first make sure, yes, that our first responders have the resources for the fastest response to put out the fires as fast as possible. We have to address things like the blocked fire hydrants that you keep raising with us in conversations. But second, we need to also expand public education immediately, right? The things that you raised during the press conferences, the closing– the doors that weren't closed behind, we need to, you know, make sure we're highlighting that and reaching the audiences in the Bronx, in Queens, in the neighborhoods that are really impacted. But third, and this is where I am the Chair of the Housing Committee on the Council, we have to make sure we're having a conversation that also puts the onus on the owners of these old properties to address the failing systems leading to these fires. At 226 West Tremont, it's an old building, that owner is the fourth worst in the City of New York. And in the last year, the building had 13 violations for defective and missing smoke detectors, which meant— means that the city was– that the residents were calling it in. And in the last two weeks, there were violations for

self-closing doors. So the, the second question— the first question was about data. The second question is about the interagency coordination. How is FDNY sharing everything in real time that you're seeing about fires and causes? How are you talking about that with the Department of Buildings, with HPD, and crafting new policies and new interventions to address the root causes? And finally, you know, as we talk about the infrastructure in these buildings, I just want to make sure that that is also a part of the conversation. And I think I mentioned this to you, Commissioner and Chief, in some of the Zooms we had. When FDNY has all the press in front of you, because there's been a fatal fire and there's been a tragedy, just making sure that the agency does not then only talk about the self-closing doors and the smoke detectors, the interventions that the tenants are responsible for, because that feels like blaming the victims. It feels like you're blaming, by only focusing on those causes. It feels like a blame on, on our people in the Bronx. And I want to make sure that one, we are doing, right? We are— HPD, DOB, FDNY are collaborating on solutions, but we're also

talking about what owners can do. So one, data. Two– now I am forgetting what my second question was, but I'm sure you captured it and I'll bring it back around if you didn't.

So I, I'll just take a couple and then, Chief could jump in here. So, one, the collaboration, right, between DOB, HPD, FDNY, we are collaborating, and there is no strategy that we won't, you know, try to get this message out there. We have done collaborative PSAs. I've done PSAs with the Commissioner of Aging. I've done PSAs with Commissioner— the DOB Commissioner. The mayor himself put out PSAs for us. We had him do a PSA because he has a large following. So he's done a PSA for us. We have life safety pamphlets and different things out there. We're working together to try to solve a problem because we know that lives are attached to this, right? We know that people are going to die if we don't get this message out, if they don't understand how to behave if they actually get into a fire situation. Now, we don't want them to get into into a fire situation, which is why we talk about things like overloading outlets, overloading

power strips. We talk about not putting your space heater too close to things that are combustible. And, you know, I can appreciate what you're saying as far as how do we talk about this when we're in the press. When we're in the press, there are a couple things we have to hit, right? We have to give them strategies, give the people strategies so that they can share that information amongst themselves if they get into a place where they're in an emergency situation. And it's not intended to put blame on anybody, but if we have these situations where these violations exist and our fire prevention, uh, folks go in there and they write those violations too, right? But if those places exist and those violations exist already, I mean, telling the owners is not necessarily going to solve the problem in the press. Telling the people what they should be getting, informing them of how your door should work, how your– you know, how your apartment– how you're supposed to have fire smoke alarms. That is the stuff that gets them calling 311, gets them reporting the building, you know, reporting their issues to the supers and the landlords. We want them to be as educated as possible, and we will do

anything we can to try to keep these folks safe. Um, we give smoke alarms. We install smoke alarms, we want people to know that, that if you need smoke alarms, we can do that for you. You can call 311 and say, I need smoke alarms, and we can come and make that happen. We want people to know that their doors are supposed to close behind them. And a lot of people rig it so it doesn't, because they don't want to get locked out if they walk out into the hallway. We want them to know these things, because these are the things that keep them safe. So, we certainly don't want to put blame on the victim, but we want to educate the victim and give them as much information so that they can share it with their families and friends and be safe if, God forbid, they end up in a position where they're trying to survive in a fire situation. As far as the data, you can— you can give the data.

So for multiple alarm fires in the Bronx, at this time, as of May 13th this year, we've had 27 multiple fires— multiple alarm fires. On May 13th, 2025, we were at 16, and May

13th, 2024, we were at 12. So— a significant increase, as we've said before.

Thank you. Chair, may I just ask a quick follow-up? We're on the same team here. We want, you know, the— we want New Yorkers to be safe and avoid these situations. On that vein, FDNY, you folks throw yourselves at the hardship. You throw yourself at the emergency. So let me take it to the– to a different place, which is what information does FDNY share with buildings and HPD? And are you actively— at the FDNY executive level, are you actively talking about, hey, buildings are having electrical shorts all over the place, you all should really have this in your scopes of work when you're putting out preservation grants or tax incentives? Are you having that conversation with agencies? Because from the— as the Housing Chair, it does not feel like what we're getting on the Council, what we're approving, the scopes of work that we're approving for tax incentives are not covering these electrical causes of fires. So, I just want to understand what the conversation is.

Thank you for your question. We recently met with the commissioner of DOB and discussed those issues. Electrical fires have been consistently the leading cause of fire within the city, and our buildings continue to get older and older, and we continue to see these electrical fires. We are working on developing new technologies that may potentially alert us to these fires prior to them occurring. There are some, you know, hopeful items out there that we're going to work on and work with some national laboratories. We've already consulted with Underwriters Laboratory to try to develop some of these products for use within the city. Obviously, we are a huge city with a complicated set of buildings here. We're one of the oldest cities in the nation. So, we do work with other agencies as well and make sure that we address these problems prior to them starting. And as to the Commissioner's point, we never want to blame anybody for any actions that cause these fires, but we do want to make sure we take that risk with the idea that somebody else won't die. And fire prevention does a tremendous job to

issue violations prior to the fire as well as after the fire. So we do do a post-fire inspection, and all those violations do go to the owner of the building. And a lot of those issues that we addressed at the press conference, those are directly related to the fire that just occurred right before that press conference occurred. So we want to strike while the iron's hot, and we— some of those things we don't know at the time of the press conference either. Like, we have our marshals go out and they investigate whether the smoke detectors were installed properly. That's not information we may have at the time of those press conferences, so we want to make sure that we get the information out to the building residents immediately so that doesn't occur again.
Thank you. Thank you, Chairs, for the time.
Thank you. Okay, we have Council Member Maloney followed by Council Member Gennaro.
My question is just high-rise buildings because there are a lot. I'm not a big fan—
[interposing] Oh wait, Maloney, sorry, Council Member Maloney.
I'm sorry, go ahead.

All right. Thank you for being here. I wanted to return to the question about EMS retention and the career pipeline there. One of the challenges you've already alluded to is significant workforce turnover and difficulties with both recruitment and retention for EMS. What percent of EMS are leaving each year, and what percent of those leaving are heading to the FDN– or to fire?

Yes, so the attrition rate last year was about 10.9 percent, and the annualized attrition rate for this year is about 14.3 percent. That's much higher than it would be in a year in which there weren't firefighter promos. So in years without firefighter promos, the attrition rate is closer to seven or eight percent.
Okay. So you roughly— what percent would you say is converting to FDNY roles? Seven?

Converting to FDNY, to firefighter? During a promotion cycle, which is multiple classes, they're all coming from a promo list, so they go consecutively. We will shift about 25 percent of the EMS workforce from EMS into fire.
And what percent of the incoming firefighter academy class then would be from EMT or EMS?
It'll be a promotion— it'll be a promotion class for the most part. So that entire group of people who left EMS will end up being the probationary class in the fire academy.
And is the training different or the same for those two roles?

Well, there are different focuses, right? But so, you know, where the people coming from EMS have been certified as EMTs or paramedics, and they're required to recertify their EMT and paramedics every four years in order to

maintain their positions. Once they go into the fire academy, then they're taught fire-matics [sic] And they're taught firefighting, you know, curriculum. You could talk a little bit more about what you're teaching them, but it is specific to the job that they're doing. But when it comes to an operational perspective, once they've moved over from EMS to fire, outside of the CFR engine, they are no longer doing EMT-level or paramedic-level work, they're doing firefighting work, which is the stuff that they learned in the fire academy.

The current probie class that we have in the fire academy is all EMS promotions. Later in the year, we'll hire another class that 60 to 70 percent will be EMS promotions. And then what they learn in the fire academy, whether you came from EMS or not the curriculum is the same, and it's all about firefighting operations that EMS does not currently have and do.
And just so we're clear once those folks become firefighters, they're no longer working on an ambulance in any way. So they're not able to go across from fire to EMS.

So asking both questions together. One is, have you considered if it'd be more cost-effective to close that promotional pathway if the training is different? And then the other is, what role EMS compensation and increasing that compensation plays, and if that would be more cost-effective than continuously investing in recruiting and trying to retrain or train new people if you're cycling out 10 to 14 percent per year.

So, there has been lots of discussion about the promotion pathway from EMS to fire because it does take such a large chunk of EMS at one date range and put them into another area of the department. However, because of that promotion process, people come to EMS. So in order to be eligible for a promotion, you have to work at EMS for four years. So what generally happens is somebody who wants to be a firefighter will come in through EMS, spend their four years at EMS, and then look to promote into fire. So if I were to close that promotion process, that segment of people that come to EMS to become firefighters would no longer have a reason to come to EMS to become firefighters.

So without there being some significant compensation so that if you were an EMT or a paramedic, you can make the choice as to whether you want to stay in EMS or become a firefighter. That's the pay parity part, right? If the money was in place so that people didn't have to leave EMS to go to fire to make more money, then the expectation is those people would stay in EMS and we would have to train far fewer people, because right now we're training constantly and it's pretty costly to continue to train, to move people from one area that department to the other area department.
And just to close out, I know I'm out of time, but do you have an estimate of what those costs are on recruiting and training?

Yeah. So for EMT, it costs $41,000 to train, coming in the door, a new employee EMT. For a paramedic, it costs $130,000. And we train our EMTs to be paramedics. So there are people that work for us who are being upgraded to paramedic. That's $130,000. For refresher training, which is what happens every four years, for an EMT

it's $6,300, and for a medic it's $9,000. So essentially, we would save money if we had to— if we were able to keep people longer than having to keep bringing them in at the entry level.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Okay, great. So round two, we have Council Member Brewer followed by Council Member Wong.

Sorry for the mistake earlier. My question is just tall buildings. Some of your previous commissioners would bring to my attention, because on the Upper West Side there are developers who just wanna build to the sky. And the comment was we just don't have enough capacity to deal with these super talls. And I– obviously, we want development or some people want a lot of development. I want lower development. And yet, I really have no concept whether or not what was said in the past is true. Are you— is this something you're thinking about? Is there something that you're concerned about with these super talls which seem to be proliferating? So I'm just wondering about your

opinion on that. And then I didn't say earlier, I don't think that in participatory budgeting, we got a new HVAC system on Ladder 25 on 77th Street. So, Westsiders just love your members. Just want to let you know.
Well, thank you.
But in terms of the supertalls.
You wanna talk about supertalls?

So since the turn of this century, the building materials and building technology has allowed us to build smaller buildings but much taller than historically than we've been able to. And one of the issues that we face with that is it could take us longer to get from the sidewalk upstairs than it does to get from the EMS station or the firehouse to the scene. So we, you know, we do look at response times and— but these are newer-built buildings. They have auxiliary fire protection systems. They're generally more fire safe than the older buildings that we're talking about and

generally have less fire instances in them. You might have more emergencies and the same with EMS and their response time to be able to get upstairs for— to provide life-saving care. So–
So you're saying in terms of the fire, not the emergency heart attack or whatever, the fire that you're feeling that they're somewhat safe is what you're saying?
They're— well, they're more fire safe than some of the older buildings that we have.
All right, well, I appreciate that. I wish you had said the opposite, because I can't stand them, but thank you very much.
Council Member Wong, followed by Restler.

Thank you, Chairs. I— okay, do you have figures on how many EMTs left to become firefighters versus how many EMTs left to become paramedics for the past year? And is pay gap the reason, or what can we do to improve the retention rate?

Thank you. So I think I have those numbers, although I might have to look up some of them. So just in terms of how many EMS members have left to become firefighters, you know, over the last three firefighter classes, we've lost 506 members.

And I just want to— EMTs don't leave the job to become paramedics, they promote to paramedic after going through rigorous training. So they still stay on EMS. Each paramedic class, we run approximately two a year, and we graduate– we graduate about 70 from each one of those classes.
Okay. And, like, we've been talking about this since the last hearing, how do we fix this retention rate? Is that being considered in the current budget year, or is still something that's not solved?

I think the Commissioner has said it multiple times that one of the things that, you know, that would help us with retention is the EMS pay being increased, right? Like, we have members who are out there dedicated every single day

that deserve to be compensated for the work that they do. Right here in the room, we– you know, just looking around, we have an incentive program every single month. We have what we call a Unit of the Month program. That Unit of the Month, for the first time ever this month, the same unit from the Bronx has won that pro— has won that title two months in a row. And just two of those members happen to be sitting right here. I wish your counterpart was here because they actually are from his district. All right, so I think we need to recognize the work that our EMTs and our paramedics do, and they should be compensated for it.
But in the current budget, the EMS pay levels remain the same. Is that right?

Yes. So, as of this point, these conversations are still happening between OLR, OMB, and the FDNY unions. They're in the contract negotiations now, and I don't have a seat at that table. So, you know, it's a an ongoing conversation. It's a conversation we continue to bring light to because we do believe it's step one to

stabilizing the EMS system, which, you know, as the Chief spoke about and Chief Miano has spoken about is a real thing. Like, I think at this point we need to stabilize our EMS system and the pay is gonna be one of those things that set us on the right path to get that done. And possibly then we can look at promotion processes, right? So if there is an option to stay in EMS, somebody may take that. But right now we have a 17,000-person department who are willing to do just about anything to keep New Yorkers safe. They'll do it in good weather and bad weather. They'll do it in any time of year. And as you've seen over the last you know, the last winter we had, which is extraordinarily cold, which caused a lot of the fires we're seeing now, or you see it during a pandemic, which was incredibly challenging. The Fire Department never turns their back on New Yorkers. So at this point, we're saying we have to prepare ourselves and build this department in a way that provides these services for the next five decades for New York.
